lessons.title: The butterfly and angles
lessons.objective: Explain the goalie's stance and how they cut down angles.

payload.prompt: Identify the butterfly save position.

image.alt: Goalie in butterfly position, pads flared to seal the ice.

options.text: Butterfly: knees down, pads flared outward.
Upright stance with pads together.
One leg extended to block the perimeter.

explanation.correct: Right. Butterfly is knees down, pads flared, sealing the net.
explanation.incorrect: The butterfly position drops both knees and spreads the pads wide.
explanation.sayThisLine: Butterfly covers the bottom of the net.

payload.prompt: A shooter comes down the wing. Where does the goalie stand to cut the angle?

options.text: On the line between the puck and the middle of the net, a step out from the goal line.
options.explanation: Correct. Standing on that line, squared to the puck, leaves the shooter the least net to see.

options.text: Deep in the net, back against the goal line.
Wide of the crease, right beside the shooter.

explanation.correct: Right. Coming out a step and staying on the line between the puck and the net's center shrinks the target. Not too far, or the shooter can go around him.
explanation.incorrect: The goalie wants to be on the line between the puck and the center of the net, a step out from the goal line. Too deep gives the shooter a big target; too wide leaves the net open.
explanation.sayThisLine: He's so square to the shooter, he's cut the angle off.

payload.prompt: A goalie who sits deep in his net gives the shooter more net to see. True or false?

scene.alt: Goalie positioning deep in the crease while a shooter approaches.

explanation.correct: True. A goalie who sits deep leaves more of the net visible. Coming out to challenge makes the shooter's target smaller.
explanation.incorrect: A goalie deep in the net gives the shooter more of the net to aim at. Challenging out shrinks that target, though going too far out invites a deke.

payload.prompt: Why does the butterfly position create rebounds?

options.text: Hard pads bounce pucks instead of absorbing them.
The goalie's chest is exposed in this position.
Goalies cannot move quickly out of the butterfly.
Shots pass through the goalie in the butterfly.

explanation.correct: Right. Pads are firm, so pucks bounce off them, while a glove or chest can absorb the shot. The butterfly covers the bottom of the net, and the price is a few more rebounds.
explanation.incorrect: The butterfly uses the hard pads to block low shots. Those pads bounce pucks away rather than absorbing them, which is where rebounds come from.
explanation.sayThisLine: The butterfly is great, but he has to control the rebound.

statement.speaker: Color commentator
statement.text: That goalie plays too deep. He is giving up angles.

payload.question: What angle problem does the commentator see?

options.text: Staying deep gives the shooter a bigger view.
options.explanation: Correct. Deep play = more net to aim at.

options.text: The goalie's pads are positioned wrong.
options.explanation: It is about positioning depth, not pad angle.

options.text: The goalie is facing the wrong way.
options.explanation: The complaint is about how deep he sits, not which way he faces.

payload.translation: Playing too deep in the crease gives shooters more of the net to aim at. Coming out a step shrinks the target.

followUps.line: Does he come out to challenge more on other shots?
followUps.why: Shows you know goalies adjust depth depending on the shot.

followUps.line: Is he afraid of getting deked if he comes out too far?
followUps.why: Shows you know there's a balance between too deep and too far out.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Angles are subtle. Asking what she sees in a goalie's positioning is a great way to learn.

lessons.title: Rebounds and second chances
lessons.objective: Explain rebound control and why second chances score.

payload.prompt: A big rebound in front often leads to a more dangerous second shot. True or false?

scene.alt: Goalie deflecting a shot; puck bounces loose in front.

explanation.correct: True. After a rebound the goalie is often out of position and the puck is loose in the slot, so a forward gets a close, quick shot.
explanation.incorrect: A big rebound is dangerous. The goalie is often out of position, and a forward nearby gets a close shot at an open net.

payload.prompt: What is a goalie's best way to kill a rebound?

options.text: Smother it with a glove or his body, or steer it to the corner.
Kick it straight back into the slot.
Let it bounce off a flat pad into the crease.

explanation.correct: Right. Smothering freezes the puck and brings a whistle; steering it to the corner sends it somewhere attackers can't reach.
explanation.incorrect: Rebounds that land in the slot or the crease are the ones forwards pounce on. Goalies either smother the puck or steer it toward the corners.

payload.prompt: Why are rebounds in the slot so dangerous?
payload.template: A rebound in the {{area}} is dangerous because the shooter is {{how}} to the net and the goalie must {{what}}.

explanation.correct: Exactly. A slot rebound gives a forward a close shot while the goalie is still moving, so there's very little time to recover.
explanation.incorrect: The slot is right in front of the net. A rebound there gives the shooter a short shot before the goalie can get set again.

payload.prompt: Order how a slot rebound becomes a goal.

items.text: A shot bounces off the goalie into the slot.
items.why: The first shot leaves a rebound in the most dangerous area.

items.text: A forward gets to the puck while the goalie is still resetting.
items.why: The goalie needs a moment to get back in position, and the forward has that moment.

items.text: A quick shot from close range beats the goalie.
items.why: A close shot at a partly open net is hard to stop.

explanation.correct: That's the order: a rebound lands in the slot, a forward gets to it while the goalie is still resetting, and he has a close shot at a mostly open net.
explanation.incorrect: It flows like this: the save leaves a rebound in the slot, a forward jumps on it before the goalie resets, and he scores from close range.

statement.speaker: Analyst
statement.text: He made the save but leaked a juicy rebound to the slot.

payload.question: What did the goalie do wrong?

options.text: Did not control the rebound properly.
options.explanation: Correct. A loose puck in scoring position is a mistake.

options.text: Did not make the first save.
options.explanation: He made the save. The problem is the rebound.

options.text: Should have called a timeout.
options.explanation: Rebound control is a skill, not a timeout situation.

payload.translation: The goalie stopped the first shot, but the puck rebounded into the most dangerous area, giving a forward a second chance.

followUps.line: Did his defense clear it, or did they score on the rebound?
followUps.why: Keeps the chat on what happened next.

followUps.line: Is he a goalie who controls his rebounds usually?
followUps.why: Shows you know rebound control is a goalie skill.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Rebound control is a skill you'll start to notice. Asking about a particular goalie is a good way in.

lessons.title: Save percentage, GAA and limits
lessons.objective: Read goalie stats and understand what they measure.

payload.prompt: Estimate the NHL's typical save percentage in recent seasons.

explanation.correct: Nice. In recent seasons the league-wide save percentage has hovered around .905, so a goalie at .915 is having a strong year.
explanation.incorrect: The typical NHL save percentage in recent seasons is about .905. Around .915 is strong, and it shifts a little from year to year.
explanation.sayThisLine: A .915 save percentage is well above the league norm.

payload.prompt: Save percentage treats every shot the same. What does that miss?

options.text: How dangerous each shot was.
How many saves the goalie made.
Whether the goalie was in net.

explanation.correct: Right. A .910 against lots of high-danger shots is a different story from a .910 against long, easy ones. Save percentage can't tell them apart.
explanation.incorrect: Save percentage is saves divided by shots, so a point-shot save counts the same as a point-blank one. Shot quality is what it misses.

payload.prompt: What does goals-against average measure?
payload.template: Goals-against average is goals allowed per {{unit}}, and it depends partly on the {{who}} in front of the goalie.

explanation.correct: Exactly. GAA is goals allowed per 60 minutes. A strong team that limits shots makes any goalie's GAA look better.
explanation.incorrect: GAA is goals allowed per 60 minutes, and it depends on how many and how good the shots are, which is partly the defense in front of the goalie.

payload.prompt: Match the goalie stat to what it measures.

pairs.definition: Saves divided by shots faced; it doesn't account for shot quality.
Goals allowed per 60 minutes; it reflects the goalie and the defense.
A team result that depends on offense and defense too, not just the goalie.

explanation.summary: Save percentage is usually the cleaner goalie number, but it still misses shot quality. GAA and wins depend heavily on the team around him.
explanation.sayThisLine: His save percentage is .915, so he's stopping most of what he sees.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: Our goalie has lower GAA, so ours is better.

payload.question: Why might this conclusion be wrong?

options.text: Our defense might be better, which lowers any goalie's GAA.
options.explanation: Correct. GAA depends partly on the defense in front, so context matters.

options.text: GAA is not counted in modern hockey.
options.explanation: GAA is still tracked, just not reliable alone.

options.text: Never compare goalies by stats.
options.explanation: Stats help. Just look at the right ones.

payload.translation: A lower GAA might come from a better defense rather than a better goalie, so it doesn't settle the question by itself.

followUps.why: Save percentage is a cleaner comparison than GAA.

followUps.line: How many shots does each team give up?
followUps.why: Shows you know shot volume feeds into GAA.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Comparing goalies is hard. Asking for the context is better than picking a side.

lessons.title: Goals saved above expected
lessons.objective: Explain how shot quality reveals true skill.

statement.speaker: Analyst
statement.text: His save percentage looks ordinary, but he faces brutal shots. His goals saved above expected are huge.

payload.question: What is the analyst saying?

options.text: He's stopping more than a shot-quality model says he should.
options.explanation: Correct. Saving more than expected on hard shots shows up as a big goals saved above expected.

options.text: His team defends well and gives up only easy shots.
options.explanation: The analyst says he faces brutal shots, so the defense isn't the story.

options.text: He has the best save percentage in the league.
options.explanation: The analyst says his save percentage looks ordinary.

payload.translation: His raw save percentage is average, but the shots he faces are tough, so he's beating what a model expects. That's what a high GSAx means.

followUps.line: Is that GSAx number steady, or just a hot stretch?
followUps.why: Shows you know one season of goalie numbers can be noisy.

followUps.line: How much of that is his team's defense?
followUps.why: Shows you know the stat tries to separate goalie from defense.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Advanced stats are still evolving. It's fine to ask how the number is built.

payload.prompt: A goalie faces 2.5 expected goals and allows 1.5. He beat the model. True or false?

scene.alt: Comparison of expected goals against and actual goals allowed.

explanation.correct: True. The shots he faced were worth 2.5 goals on average, and only 1.5 went in, so he saved about one goal above expected.
explanation.incorrect: He allowed fewer goals than the shot quality predicted: 1.5 against 2.5 expected. That's one goal saved above expected.

payload.prompt: Similar save percentages, but A faced harder shots. Who's better?

situation.narrative: Over a full season, two goalies have nearly the same save percentage, but the quality of the shots they faced was different.

facts.label: Shot quality
facts.value: A faced tougher shots than B

options.label: Goalie A: he beat the model by more
options.consequence: Saving six goals above expected against harder shots is a stronger season than saving three against easier ones.
considerations: A is six goals above expected; B is three.
Raw save percentage ignores that A's shots were harder.

options.label: Goalie B: his save percentage is higher
options.consequence: B had a good year too, but his raw number is helped by easier shots.
considerations: A higher save percentage is a fair first look.
Shot quality changes the picture.

options.label: You can't say anything from these numbers
options.consequence: Over a full season the numbers do say something, even if no stat is perfect.
considerations: Expected goals are an estimate, not a verdict.
A full season is a decent sample.

payload.expertNote: Raw save percentage treats every shot the same. Goals saved above expected adjusts for shot quality, so it can reverse the ranking. Even so, one season of goalie data is noisy.
payload.sayThisLine: His save percentage is lower, but he's facing tougher shots.

payload.prompt: Complete the GSAx definition.
payload.template: GSAx compares the goals a goalie allowed to the goals a {{model}} expected, and a positive number means he {{outcome}}.

explanation.correct: Exactly. A positive GSAx means he stopped more than a shot-quality model expected; a negative one means he let in more.
explanation.incorrect: GSAx is actual goals allowed compared with the model's expected goals against. Positive means he beat the model.

lessons.title: Starters, backups and rest
lessons.objective: Explain goalie rotation and why rest matters.

payload.prompt: Back-to-back nights and your starter is hot. Who plays?

situation.narrative: Two games in two nights, home then away. The starter is in great form and the backup hasn't played in two weeks.

facts.label: Backup
facts.value: Fresh but no games in two weeks

options.label: Play the starter both nights
options.consequence: You give yourself the best chance in both games, but a tired goalie may struggle on the second night.
considerations: The starter is hot.
Back-to-back fatigue is real.
It's more defensible late in a tight race.

options.label: Starter tonight, backup on the second night
options.consequence: The starter stays fresh for the stretch, and the backup gets game action. It's the usual way teams manage back-to-backs.
considerations: A rested starter helps across the whole season.
The backup needs game time to stay sharp.
It's a small risk on one night for a healthier goalie later.

options.label: Start the backup both nights
options.consequence: You give up your best chance in both games with a playoff race tightening, and the starter sits when he's hottest.
considerations: Rest matters, but not at the expense of both games.
The backup is rusty after two weeks off.

payload.expertNote: Most teams use the backup on one half of a back-to-back. How much they push the starter depends on the stakes.
payload.sayThisLine: They'll rest the starter on the second night of the back-to-back.

payload.prompt: What does a backup goalie usually do?
payload.template: A backup goalie often plays one game of a {{when}} so the starter can {{purpose}}.

explanation.correct: Exactly. Backups usually get one game of a back-to-back so the starter stays fresh, and they fill in when the starter is hurt.
explanation.incorrect: The backup's main job is to take some games so the starter can rest, often one night of a back-to-back.

payload.prompt: Match the workload role to its meaning.

pairs.definition: The goalie who plays most of the games, including the biggest ones.
The second goalie, who plays fewer games and fills in when the starter rests.
Two games on consecutive nights, which is when goalies often share the work.

explanation.summary: Smart teams use their backups to rest the starter, and the back-to-back is the classic spot for it.
explanation.sayThisLine: It's a back-to-back, so the backup gets the start.

payload.prompt: Five games in seven days. What is the biggest risk?

options.text: Goalie will demand a trade.
Fatigue hurts focus and positioning.
Backup will challenge for the job.
Automatic contract bonus.

explanation.correct: Right. A tired goalie is a half-step late on the angles and reads that make him good, and a tired body also gets hurt more easily.
explanation.incorrect: The main risk is fatigue: a goalie who's worn down loses the small details, like positioning and tracking rebounds.

statement.speaker: Coach
statement.text: Three back-to-backs this month. I need smart workload management.

payload.question: What is the coach planning?

options.text: Resting starter on some back-to-back nights.
options.explanation: Correct. Workload management is about spreading games between goalies.

options.text: Firing the backup if he does not perform.
Making the team play fewer games.
options.explanation: The schedule is fixed. The coach is managing what exists.

payload.translation: The coach means he'll give the backup some games, usually on back-to-backs, so the starter stays fresh for the whole season.

followUps.line: Do you trust your backup in those games?
followUps.why: Shows you know a good backup is part of a good team.

followUps.line: Do they rest him more before the playoffs?
followUps.why: Shows you know workload management is a season-long plan.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Coaches trade a bit of short-term advantage for long-term health. Asking how they think about it is fair game.

lessons.title: Interference and challenges
lessons.objective: Understand the rule and when to challenge.

payload.prompt: An attacker stands in the crease, doesn't touch the goalie, and the goalie moves freely. Interference?

scene.alt: An attacker stands in the crease beside the goalie, who has full room to move.

explanation.correct: No interference. Standing in the crease isn't enough. The question is whether the attacker impaired the goalie's ability to make the save.
explanation.incorrect: Being in the crease isn't the test. If the attacker doesn't touch the goalie or block his movement, the goal can still stand.

payload.prompt: A goal might be interference. Do you challenge?

situation.narrative: Your team just allowed a goal in the second period. An attacker brushed your goalie, but the replay is unclear.

facts.label: Replay
facts.value: Light contact, unclear if it stopped the save

facts.label: Cost of a failed challenge
facts.value: A real price for your team

options.label: Challenge; the contact was close enough
options.consequence: You might win, but borderline calls rarely get overturned, and a failed challenge costs your team.
considerations: Interference is a judgment call.
Unclear replays tend to stand as called.

options.label: Let it go and stay focused
options.consequence: You avoid the cost of a failed challenge and keep the challenge for a clearer play.
considerations: If the replay isn't clear, the call usually stands.
Choosing your spots matters.

options.label: Argue with the referee from the bench
options.consequence: The call doesn't change, and you risk a bench penalty.
considerations: Arguing doesn't start a review.
A challenge is the only formal way to ask.

payload.expertNote: Interference is a judgment call, and borderline plays rarely get overturned, so coaches save challenges for the ones where the replay is clear.
payload.sayThisLine: It wasn't clear enough to risk the challenge.

payload.prompt: What is the key question in an interference review?

options.text: Did the attacker touch the goalie?
Did it prevent a save the goalie would have made?
Was the attacker in the crease?
Did the attacker have a clear view of the net?

explanation.correct: Right. The review asks whether the attacker's contact or position kept the goalie from making the save, not just whether there was contact.
explanation.incorrect: Touching the goalie or standing in the crease isn't the test. The question is whether the attacker impaired the goalie's ability to make the save.

statement.speaker: Broadcaster
statement.text: Minimal contact but the goalie could not get across. That is interference.

payload.question: What is the broadcaster suggesting?

options.text: Light contact can still prevent a save.
options.explanation: Correct. Interference is about impact on the save, not force.

options.text: Any contact is automatic interference.
options.explanation: Not automatic. Must prevent a save.

options.text: The broadcaster thinks the goal should stand.
options.explanation: He says it's interference, which means the goal should come off the board.

payload.translation: The broadcaster thinks the contact was light but still kept the goalie from getting across, which is enough for interference.

followUps.line: Do you think they'll challenge it?
followUps.why: It keeps the chat on the next step after the call.

followUps.line: Would that have been a goal if he hadn't touched the goalie?
followUps.why: Shows you understand the test is whether the goalie could have made the save.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Interference is one of the most argued calls in hockey. It's fine to say it looks close.

payload.prompt: Order how a challenged goal gets reviewed.

items.text: A goal is scored and signaled on the ice.
items.why: The play has to happen before anyone can challenge it.

items.text: The coach decides to challenge before play restarts.
items.why: A challenge has to be made quickly, before the next faceoff.

items.text: Officials and the league's video staff study the replays.
items.why: They look at the angles that show the contact or the entry.

items.text: The referee announces whether the goal stands or is waved off.
items.why: Play doesn't restart until the ruling is announced.

explanation.correct: That's the order: the goal, the challenge, the video review, then the ruling.
explanation.incorrect: It runs goal, then challenge before play restarts, then video review, and finally the referee announces the ruling.
